messages.author: 0a6a9c49b017f046
messages.subject: vectorizing multi-level hierarchical models
parts:
Dear Stan users,

I fit kinetic parameters of subjects which have different treatments assigned. Per treatment I have a (possibly) varying number of subject such that I end up writing model code like this:

for(i in 1:S) {
alpha[i] ~ normal(mu_alpha[SC[i]], sigma_alpha[SC[i]]);
beta[i] ~ normal(mu_beta[SC[i]], sigma_beta[SC[i]]);
}

Here, S is the total number of subjects and SC is the subject to category/treatment mapping. As you can see, this is brute force for-looping. So is it possible to specify ranges for vectors and make vectorized statements like this:

alpha[ subject-range category 1 ] ~ normal(mu_alpha[1], sigma_alpha[1])
alpha[ subject-range category 2 ] ~ normal(mu_alpha[2], sigma_alpha[2])

and so on. I saw that Eigen has support for vector.segment, so this kind of array indexing should be possible.

Best,

Sebastian

BTW, has someone tried to get Eigens support for the Intel MKL running with Stan?

--

messages.subject: Re: vectorizing multi-level hierarchical models
parts:
On Wednesday, October 17, 2012 8:26:08 AM UTC-4, Sebastian Weber wrote:
I fit kinetic parameters of subjects which have different treatments assigned. Per treatment I have a (possibly) varying number of subject such that I end up writing model code like this:

   for(i in 1:S) {
      alpha[i] ~ normal(mu_alpha[SC[i]], sigma_alpha[SC[i]]);
      beta[i] ~ normal(mu_beta[SC[i]], sigma_beta[SC[i]]);
   }

Here, S is the total number of subjects and SC is the subject to category/treatment mapping. As you can see, this is brute force for-looping. So is it possible to specify ranges for vectors and make vectorized statements like this:

alpha[ subject-range category 1 ] ~ normal(mu_alpha[1], sigma_alpha[1])
alpha[ subject-range category 2 ] ~ normal(mu_alpha[2], sigma_alpha[2])

and so on. I saw that Eigen has support for vector.segment, so this kind of array indexing should be possible.

It is one thing to say that Eigen or C++ supports something and another thing to get the Stan parser to produce the corresponding C++ code. I guess you could use the Stan parser to generate a .cpp file and then manually edit the .cpp file to change those two lines to be more efficient. Note that your parameters may be std::vectors rather than Eigen objects, but you could hack in whatever iterators are valid for a std::vector. If you come up with something really good, let us know and Bob might be able to implement it in the parser.
BTW, has someone tried to get Eigens support for the Intel MKL running with Stan?

Several months ago, I once verified that our tests work with the Intel MKL compiler. I didn't really test if code runs faster, but it certainly takes longer for the Intel MKL compiler to compile Stan code, which has lots of templates and metaprogramming. I don't think I defined whatever it is that makes Eigen use Intel MKL but it would probably work. The thing is that you would have to define that before compiling the whole Stan library, in addition to the specific model you are trying to estimate.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: vectorizing multi-level hierarchical models
parts:
Most of our compute time is spent in auto-dif
and the rest in expensive function eval (log,
exp, lgamma, etc.)

You'll find that every matrix/array access, etc.,
uses a + 1 to index from 1. This is really inefficient
compared to using iterators, but the cost of the +1 is
a negligible cost in the overall Stan code, so eliminating
it won't lead to much of a speedup.

There are lots of other places where iteration can
be sped up, but I seriously doubt it'll lead to
any measurable improvements in speed.

- Bob
